utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I already asked the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom, on the assumption that there are no procedural matters to be raised at this moment. At this same time, I'd like you -- yes, but first, Mr. Registrar, could you already prepare exhibit numbers, provisionally, for the Defence exhibits that have been used during the examination of Mr. Vasic. If you prepare it and we'll hear later from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Two procedural matters: First an inquiry. I just wanted to ask precisely what time the Court intends to adjourn today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Approximately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll finish 55 minutes earlier than usual, that's 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And secondly, the Court asked yesterday about the census, and may recall that the Prosecution volunteered to provide that exhibit. We have that today and are prepared to tender it at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's there. I think we had better at this moment first use our time, because we are close to the end of a couple of days, and if there's any time left, we can distribute it, but it's good to know that it's there and ready to be submitted and ready to be admitted. Mr. Tieger, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Vasic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Tieger, who is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to remind, Mr. Vasic. Mr. Vasic, you're still bound by the solemn declaration you made last Monday at the beginning of your testimony. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the process may be expedited by the distribution of a binder containing certain documents that may be used during the course of the cross-examination, including one that should be presented to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, the binder that has just been placed on the table in front of you contains certain documents that we may be referring to during the course of this examination. I will, of course -- it's tabbed with certain numbers, and when necessary, I'll refer you to a particular tab and then you can direct your attention to the document. I'd like to begin by asking you about some of the factors that might have led to the departure of Muslims from Prnjavor. First of all, acts such as harassment at gunpoint, being stopped on a discriminatory basis at checkpoints, and various forms of abuse would be the kinds of events that would encourage people to leave the municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this was not something that was done selectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm having some trouble hearing the translation, although I'll play with the equipment now and see -- and continue, see if that works.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear us better now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you're now asked whether you would hear the interpreters better, but it seems that you do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me try that one more time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One, two, three, testing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger smiles, so that's on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The types of activity that I just catalogued represent exactly what Veljko Milankovic and the Wolves of Vucjak were doing in 1991 and 1992; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of the fact that checkpoints were set up by the police and the armed forces. And as to people being stopped by the Wolves or any other formations, probably yes, but I'm not aware of that. But yes, of course I can say that your claim would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that would certainly represent a reason why Muslims in Prnjavor would be encouraged to leave the municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims from Prnjavor left mostly in 1995, and in the meantime, Muslim refugees actually used to come to Prnjavor. We have it documented. 350 refugees from another place came along and I took the risk upon myself and got the Crisis Staff to decide to accept them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Irrespective of the exodus of Muslims in 1995 and the reasons for that, it is correct that the kind of activity that I indicated earlier would make the Muslims of Prnjavor feel insecure and would encourage them to leave the municipality; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody felt unsafe, and whoever could leave, left. Some Muslims amongst them, but I explained that in my testimony earlier on. At any rate, illegal checkpoints would cause fear and would cause fear to Muslims as well, amongst others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And more specifically, Veljko Milankovic and the Wolves of Vucjak were provoking and harassing the Muslim population; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were individual cases which were documented, but sanctions were imposed on those people who were reported, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we'll get to that a bit later, but rather than bearing the brunt of sanctions, it's correct that Veljko Milankovic became a hero who was praised and lionised by the leaders of the SDS and Republika Srpska; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Veljko Milankovic, as a fighter, was well-liked by the Serb people, because he made his name on the battlefield. And it was an incredible burden to us, because almost the entire unit, in the end, was seen to have been killed, and most of those killed from Prnjavor were from that unit, and they were mostly young men between 18 and 20 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's focus for a moment, if we can, not on his activity in legitimate forms of combat but on his activities directed toward the Muslim population. And in that connection, I'd ask you to turn to tab 2 of the binder, which contains a report by CSB chief Stojan Zupljanin in September of 1991. And if I could direct your attention to various parts of that document.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already read it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, the day before, three days ago maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I take it you noted in the report the information about gunfire, illegal searches, provocations, senseless acts of malice on innocent citizens, and the report that particularly characteristic in that respect was Veljko Milankovic's group; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only during that initial period, and we have already talked about the arrests of people from that group. The authorities of the municipality of Prnjavor fully cooperated with the police force in imposing sanctions. Because at that point, they were not a military formation as yet. This happened after their return from training in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as noted, approximately the eighth paragraph, Milankovic and his group provoked and harassed the Muslim population with the aim of precipitating inter-ethnic fighting during that period of time; right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be interpreted that way. And in the same way they provoked and disturbed the Serb population as well, because here, in the first paragraph, it says in villages and at religious meetings, and this is a reference to what was happening in Serb villages, in fact, and they were arrested for that type of behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I certainly wasn't suggesting that Mr. Milankovic was incapable of engaging in criminal activity toward Serbs, but the report couldn't be clearer, Mr. Vasic, could it, that Milankovic's activities were primarily directed toward or selectively directed toward the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who drafted this report obviously thought so. In these cases described here, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you've talked not only about his criminal activity toward Muslims, but also some similar conduct toward Serbs. It's true, in fact, that the Wolves were characterised by and replete with people of, let's say, low morals; isn't that right, led by Milankovic, who was a repeat criminal offender.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information that I received initially, no, but at a later stage, when volunteers came from other municipalities as well, at that stage, yes. But at that stage, they were already turned into a military formation. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in fact, these were people who displayed hatred of non-Serb people and who reflected a genocidal element; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Those aren't my words, Mr. Vasic; those are the words of Colonel Tolimir of the VRS. Let me ask you to turn to tab 18 of the document -- of the binder, rather. As you can see from the first pages, this is a report to the Main Staff, VRS Main Staff, dated July 28th, 1992, and it's signed by Colonel Zdravko Tolimir, as reflected on the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you are referring to the tabs. Perhaps for the record it would be wise that if a document like tab 2 is already in evidence, that for the record you would just remind us under what number is has been admitted, because it will not be admitted again. So tab 2 was P364.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clearly listed, but perhaps for the record, if anyone later on has to read it, knows exactly where to find the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course. And thanks for that reminder. In that connection, I should note that tab 18, the document to which I just referred, is P529, tab 463.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, as you can see from the first paragraph, Mr. Vasic, this is a report on paramilitary formations in the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this report, as the last page indicates, was directed, in addition to the president of the Presidency, to the Prime Minister, and as I indicated, to the Main Staff commander. Colonel Tolimir describes the main characteristics of these groups in the second full paragraph of the report, noting "They are mostly comprised of individuals of low moral quality, and in many cases, of persons previously prosecuted for crimes and offences and even convicted for various crimes ..." that he lists, including murder. He goes on to note that: "Many formations of this type display hatred of non-Serbian peoples, and one can conclude without reservations that are the genocidal element among the Serbian people." And finally, let me direct your attention to the page number 4 of the English, which would be, I believe, your same page as well in the original B/C/S. Tolimir goes on to note the most important of these groups, indicating that: "The detachment of Veljko Milankovic from Prnjavor has about 150 men and is, as of recently, formally under the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. Members of this detachment are involved in extensive looting and recently attacked the Tactical Group 3rd Command Post -" or 3 Command Post - "arresting one Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina Army colonel in the process." Colonel Tolimir is directing his attention and the attention of the Main Staff, the president of the Presidency, and the Prime Minister to the same group we've been talking about, correct, the group led by Veljko Milankovic, which operated out of Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document tells you to what extent the military was disorganised, because this is a report which is drafted by the Main Staff and this is already the time when Wolves from Vucjak were incorporated into one of the formations of the Republika Srpska army. I think it was within the 1st Corps, commanded by General Talic. And even before that, orders were issued by General Uzelac. As far as I know, military never issued orders to paramilitary formations, and Colonel Tolimir does say here that they were formally already included in the armed forces of the Republic of Srpska. And this attack on the commander of the Tactical Group 3, as far as we know, happened on the front line, not in Prnjavor itself. And that tells us something about disagreements within the army amongst themselves. As to whether there was any other reason or any other background to that conflict, I do not know, but this already is an example. And even before that time and even on the basis of the records referring to the soldier that we looked at yesterday, that they were already incorporated within the armed forces, and Tolimir does not argue with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There's nothing in Tolimir's report that disagrees with what you said. He said that the Wolves of Vucjak were recently formally incorporated, and we'll look at that document later. And as you noted, he doesn't seem to dispute the fact that the army, prior to that time, was willing to use Veljko Milankovic and the Wolves of Vucjak in their operations; right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see this as a reflection of how misinformed he was of what was going on within the 5th Corps of the Republika Srpska armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel Tolimir seems to be very well-informed about quite a number of groups, as you look through the report. He certainly knows about the recent subordination of Milankovic and the Wolves of Vucjak, and he knows a great deal about the composition of the group and their character; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and he does say that the other formations are paramilitary formations, and he says that this one is a part of the military. And I myself said in my statement that initially when they only had 20 to 30 members, and when they stayed on the territory of the municipality, apart from Veljko, others were mostly young men who were not criminals. And afterwards, when they joined the army and when the unit was enlarged and more volunteers joined in, criminals as well joined in from other municipalities. But that was within the area of competence of the military, and in my statement yesterday I did say that the biggest problem to the civilian authorities was the fact that basically on a daily basis, at any given moment on the territory of the municipality of Prnjavor, we had more than a thousand fighters fully armed, and we never managed to obtain for them to have to leave their arms and weapons behind when they came and leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to turn your attention next to an article that appeared in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. I want to turn your attention to an article that appeared in Javnost, but I wonder if you would first confirm that Javnost was the publication of first the SDS, that it was established by the SDS and later became the publication of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you are right. However, I cannot say that for a fact, because I did not participate in all this, and I may have seen one or two issues of the publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Veljko Milankovic, in fact, was rather closely associated with the SDS, and in fact made financial contributions to the SDS in the period 1990 through 1992, let's say.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Veljko never gave, and he never asked for anything from the SDS, because the SDS did not have its own funds at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask --

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can somebody who has just come out of prison give money to somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you to take a quick look at tab 21, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe this is a new document, if you want to give it a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, would you assign a --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 21, Your Honours, would be P945.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, this is a July 1996 -- excuse me. This is a 1993 article from Javnost, discussing Mr. Milankovic and the Wolves, and it indicates in the first paragraph that he was a financier and connected to the local SDS leadership. It also goes on to note the training that he participated in and his own training of young men from Prnjavor and surrounding areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to my learned friend, it really is, in my submission, no good to ask a question as the witness is trying to read the documents. If he hasn't read this one before, he needs to be allowed to read it. Because asking a question through the headphones as he's reading it is really asking too much of any person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I take it that you'll take into account that if the witness first reads, that he should not be confused, unless you would like to read a certain portion of it. That, of course, would be different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was more in the nature of directing the witness's attention to a certain portion, but I certainly accept counsel's comments and I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, let me indicate I'm only going to be asking you a couple of questions --

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that I see this for the first time. This is a very poetic description of things, written by people who attended a funeral, which is obviously an event loaded with emotions. It is indisputable that Milankovic was considered a hero. He died in battle and he is still respected and loved by the Serbian people. But it is also indisputable that only the best things are said about people at their funerals and many things are exaggerated. I have not been able to find the place here where it says that he financed the SDS. However, at that time, the SDS was a movement of the Serbian people, and everybody funded it and supported it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, if you would listen to Mr. Tieger's question and answer those questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, didn't the endorsement and acceptance and use of Veljko Milankovic and the Wolves of Vucjak send a clear message to the Muslim population of Prnjavor and the surrounding areas that the kind of treatment they received from Milankovic and the Wolves reflected their Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. level of security in the areas that he operated in? In other words, sent a clear message to them that they were unwelcome and unsafe in those areas?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you are looking at Milankovic and the Wolves, and they were just members of some other formations. Their popular name was the Wolves. And the non-Serbian population probably found it equally uncomfortable to see any soldier of the Republika Srpska army if they were thinking differently than a citizen of the Republika Srpska should have been thinking. And everybody is afraid to see somebody carrying arms. I don't think that they found it any different in terms of how they felt when they saw a member of the Wolves or when they saw a member of any other unit. But I agree; I also found it very uncomfortable to see a group of ten drunken people carrying arms, and there were plenty of such scenes at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe you mentioned earlier that Milankovic and the Wolves were praised by various Bosnian Serb leaders. That would include, would it not, Mr. Krajisnik and yourself?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember ever having awarded or gave praise or anything else. I'm proud that such a fighter was amongst the ranks of the army and everything that he gave on the front line, because he gave his life to defend the Serbian people. I don't want to comment upon his criminal past before the war, though, and I'm not saying that there's anything disputable about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me just look quickly at a couple of the tabs. First tab 20, which contains an article from Glas Srpski dated 18 February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That will need a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The original and B/C/S, Your Honours, of tab 20 will be P946, and the English translation will be 946.1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just noting quickly, that article reflects remarks by you about Mr. Milankovic at his funeral, in which you said: "For everything he did, Veljko deserved to be a hero of Republika Srpska. Let us wish that he rests in peace and pray to God that his soul reaches the heavenly kingdom. We promise that many names and institutions shall bear his name in his hometown of Prnjavor, as well as in other Serbian towns." That was an accurate reflection of your remarks at that time, Mr. Vasic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. And the authorities that replaced me gave a name to -- the name of Veljko Milankovic to a street in Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I misdirected you to the tab number earlier. If you could turn to tab 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's P749, tab 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's an event that took place on the fifth anniversary of the establishment of the Wolves, according to the article. And again, it's an article from Javnost dated, in this instance, 27 July 1996, and it reflects, among other things, the remarks of Commander Mirko Sikarac, about whom you spoke earlier, talking about the training in Knin and the first operation of the Wolves in taking over the relay station on Kozara. I believe you see that in the third paragraph. And it also reflects the remarks of Mr. Krajisnik at that event, stating that: "Since 1991 when you lighted a fire of freedom by defending the people of Serbian Krajina ..." and then going on to state that: "Your deeds are immortal. You are the heroes of the third Serbian uprising and you belonged to the whole Serbian nation! We were the Wolves and we will remain the Wolves, for all those who want to take away freedom and Republika Srpska from our people." And did you hear those remarks or read about them at the time, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the election rally of the SDS. The party would use any religious gatherings or other rallies when there were a lot of people, and that's where they held their election campaign. It was well known that the anniversary of the Wolves would gather a lot of people, and the leadership of the SDS asked us to help them with the election campaign. I was informed of that. I don't know whether I've already told you that or not, I was a candidate for an MP on behalf of the Assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to return to the factors that caused people to -- caused Muslims to leave Prnjavor a bit later, but while we're on the subject of Milankovic, I want to talk about some events in Prnjavor, including Lisnja and disarming. First of all, I wanted to ask you a question about one of the tabs, one of the exhibits you produced for the Court during the course of your examination-in-chief, and that was initially tab 7, which depicts a series of photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the witness the other binder in front of him? If not, he should be provided with it. Mr. Tieger is drawing your attention to the photo documentation under tab 7, dating from June 1992, in relation to Lisnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, looking at the cover page, entitled "foto dokumentacija," I'm not sure that there's a section marked Predmet and I'm not sure that you read what the title of this photo documentation is. Can you just read that to the Court so it can be translated?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Trenches and shelters."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I take it this was not part of your personal collection of materials, or was it?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you gather these materials in preparation for coming to Court?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And from whom did you obtain them?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the chief of the public security station, the then-chief of the public security station. Yes, he was actually chief at the time. His name is Radislav Vincic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what did you ask him for? Did you ask him specifically for photographs of shelters or did you ask him for all documentation he had related to the events in Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few people who were in certain positions during the war have already come here to testify in the Brdjanin case. Some expected that they would be called as witnesses, and obviously they collected some documentation that might have come useful in this Court. I did not contact only Mr. Vincic, but also others, to see what they have and that I did not have. I wanted my evidence to be as complete as possible. That's how he told me that, with regard to the Lisnja case, he had some documents, and this is what he gave to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So as far as you know, this represents the total of all the relevant information - photos or otherwise - about events in Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These documents are part of the investigation that was conducted by the public security station of Prnjavor. According to the chief, another part of the investigation was conducted by the military services, because a military unit was involved in the investigation and they were in charge of one part of it. I don't know how they split the job amongst themselves. I don't even know who was re-subordinated to whom during that investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Apart from these photographs, are you aware of any other photos or videos depicting preparations -- depicting what you called preparations for possible combat operations, or whatever, by Muslims in Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the beginning of your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure. Are you aware of any other photographs that show preparations other than these?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the witness had not answered one of your previous questions. What did you ask for, Mr. Tieger asked you; all of the documentation? And then you gave a long answer saying that you also, in order to have the material as complete as possible, you also addressed others. But what did you ask for to Mr. Vincic? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For Mr. Vincic, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked him to show me what he has and what he could give me that could help me with my testimony. And he told me that these are the documents that he has about the Lisnja case, and this is what he gave me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you ever seen any other photographs, as asked by Mr. Tieger? Not whether you have them in your possession, but whether you have ever seen them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I've never seen any other photos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what did the other people who you said might have other sources you addressed? Did they give you anything, any material on the Lisnja events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other people are the president of the executive board, who obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking whether --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they didn't, because nobody can have more material than the chief of the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why did you then address them, if no one could have any additional material, after you had addressed already the chief of the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not address them only with Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. regard to the Lisnja case. I wanted my material to be as complete as possible in every other aspect. The president of the executive board might have had some minutes that I didn't have of some meetings. I did that in a haste, because it was only seven days prior to my coming here that I actually learned that I would be called as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I know you don't purport to be a military expert, but wasn't it plain to you when you received these photographs that they depict efforts by people to protect their homes or themselves against attack?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened much before the beginning of the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and every type of armament - illegal arming, that is - was a crime. And the same applies to digging trenches. I didn't know about the trenches before, nor was I supposed to know, but there was intelligence data about a large-scale arming of the population of Lisnja. Before the beginning of conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there could be no word about any defence. I don't know what kind of defence could one be talking about. I don't know who the aggressor might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned large-scale arming. Didn't the SDS arm Serbs on a large scale, allegedly to protect against an impending genocide?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could you please specify whether your question relates to Prnjavor or has a wider context.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask the question in two parts, if I may. Didn't the SDS arm Serbs on a large scale all over the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and also specifically in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS did not arm the population. Maybe some people did that, but not with the approval or under the auspices, so to say, of the SDS. I also received information that a group led by the SPO distributed arms, but I never learnt the details of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you about a couple of speeches by top officials in the SDS concerning that very issue that this Chamber has had the opportunity to see. First of all -- and these are both documents contained in the Treanor material, I believe, at binder 64 and binder 65. I may have to get this -- I may have to clarify the specific tab number for the Court later, but it refers to two Assembly sessions, first the 34th, and later the 50th, which were -- which Mr. Treanor directed his attention to. The first are -- represent remarks by General Gvero at the 34th session of the Assembly of the Serbian people, held in September of 1993. General Gvero noted initially that "for more than a year and a half, the Serbian people in Republika Srpska have been waging a defensive and liberation war." He talked about the Serbian Democratic Party, which "politically awakened and homogenised the Serbian people, formulated the political and social goals, and prepared all the important prerequisites for a successful struggle," and then noted in addition, or among other things, that "the Serbian Democratic Party and the established state institutions also have the most credit for the initial arming of the Serbian people with small arms." And if I could also direct your attention to the remarks of Dr. Karadzic at the 50th session of the Assembly, held in April of 1995, and during a part of his remarks he noted that when war broke out, the SDS was in power in municipalities where Serbs were a majority and had everything under their control. And then, as part of that, he noted that: "Thanks to the JNA, weapons were distributed to the Serbian people, but it was the SDS that created the army and organised the people." And finally, let me direct your attention to -- first of all, let me ask if you are aware that, first, Bosnian Serb leaders acknowledged and indeed boasted about the arming of Serb people before the war and whether that refreshes your recollection that such arming took place.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member of the Assembly. I never attended any sessions of the Assembly of the Serbian People. What General Gvero said obviously was meant to explain that the SDS homogenised the Serbian people and Radovan Karadzic said that there were no Chetniks or partisans, and the purpose of those words was to try and reconcile a vast number of the supporters of the SDS with the Serbian communists in order to unify them in defence of that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, may I draw your attention to the question put to you. The question is whether you were aware of these things having been said. You did not answer the question. You told us that you are not a member of the Assembly, which then perhaps we should understand to be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not -- I'm not aware of anything. Maybe this applied to the municipalities where the Serbs were not in power. We did not need that. The Serbs were in power and we could always distribute the arms of the regular TO. I've answered your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked whether you knew about it. Whether you are a member of parliament, sometimes I even know what happens in my parliament in my own country without being a member of parliament. So the question was whether you are aware what you did is at length interpret what might have been meant by those who are speaking. That was not asked. If there's anyone who would be interested to know your interpretation of what's said at that time, they'll certainly, whether it will be Defence, whether it will be Prosecution, whether it will be the Judges, they'll ask for it. Please focus on the questions and answer them. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you again -- please.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that because I was not present, and we received the Official Gazette; however, the Official Gazettes did not carry any speeches. They only carried conclusions and decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were you aware from any other source about arming of Serbs in order -- for the purpose of -- or for the alleged purpose of preventing genocide, or for any other reason?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were rumours, always, and if anything was done, it was done illegally. But I don't know anything about that. In Prnjavor, the SDS did not do any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. And setting aside Prnjavor for the moment, were you aware that more generally, the Bosnian Serb leadership was ensuring that the Bosnian Serbs were armed?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have any official contacts in that sense. And rumours are not something to be talked about before this Court. If I need to comment on rumours, I can do so, if you ask me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vasic, we looked at comments by Dr. Karadzic and General Gvero, talking retrospectively about the arming of Serbs. Did you also, after 1991 and 1992, praise the SDS for having armed the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I can't remember, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, please, to tab 23, which contains an article from Nas Zavicaj of September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I believe this needs a new number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 23, Your Honours, will be P947, and the English translation will be P947.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, this contains an introductory speech by you at the 16th session of the Prnjavor Municipal Assembly. I'll give you a moment to cast your eye on it, but I will indicate to you that I'll be directing your attention to the first full paragraph under the heading "Good personnel policy." And there, Mr. Vasic, you say: "We are aware of the fact that the SDS played a key role in bringing down the previous authorities, as well as in the prevention of a genocide against the Serbian people by having armed it on time, and by bridging a period between the transformation of the army from the JNA to the Serbian army." Mr. Vasic, you not only knew about such arming, but you praised the SDS and, indirectly or impliedly, yourself by having done so; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I myself and the SDS authorities who made the decision for the TO defence weapons to be distributed to the population, mostly to Serbs. Because I was not referring to any illegal arming of the population; I was referring to the TO weapons that had been distributed before the breakout of any conflicts, at the time when there was an imminent danger of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I raised that for a couple of reasons.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I raise that for a couple of reasons, Mr. Vasic, but in part in response to your comment about the shelters that are depicted in the photos. And I understood you to ask rhetorically why people would build such shelters, what did they have to be apprehensive of, who was armed? The Serbs were armed in Prnjavor, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose I made myself clear when I said that the TO -- that the Territorial Defence weapons were distributed to everyone, not in a selective manner. Those weapons were distributed to both Serbs and Muslims at the time when there was an imminent threat of war. It was the weapons that were under the control of the Territorial Defence, and according to the legal provisions, they were supposed to be used in order to guard and ensure safety of property and people, et cetera. But they were not building shelters; they were building trenches. You might not be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. familiar with the military terminology, but behind every trench there is a shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I didn't understand you before to be claiming that kind of military expertise, so we'll go into that in just a moment. But let me ask you first: It's correct, isn't it, that the Serbs in Prnjavor had overwhelming military superiority?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially, the Territorial Defence weapons, according to the relevant rules and regulations, was distributed to all the Territorial Defence units. But illegal arms were very much present in the village of Lisnja, according to all the intelligence reports from both the police and the army. And it turned out to be correct afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We've had an opportunity to see some of the judgements against persons for illegal possession of arms and other crimes. Are you suggesting to this Court that, in light of the existence of the JNA and then later the VRS, in light of the number of Serbs in Prnjavor, and in particular, the number of Serbs you told us were walking around with weapons, that there was any question about who had military superiority in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the conflict broke out, people were not thinking about possible conflict, but the arms were distributed according to the Territorial Defence law of a need such as of guardian of facilities and infrastructures, such as bridges, et cetera, and also people, individuals. That's what it says in the legal provisions. I can't remember it, I don't know it by heart, but considering that -- I can't remember the exact figure, but I think about 2.000 people were members of the Territorial Defence units in the municipality, and therefore it is only natural that more Serbs had weapons than Muslims. But that is the weapons under the control of the Territorial Defence. The problem was not the Territorial Defence weapons, in fact, but illegal weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Serb villages have shelters, sandbags at their windows, holes to crawl in by their houses?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody was building shelters, and the trenches were being made in the village of Lisnja, trenches for the purpose of fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could I ask for a few clarifications on the document P99 147. You explained to us that in your speech you referred to general distributions of TO arms to, well, the population, or from whatever. I'm trying to understand your explanation. In this speech, as we find it written down in this document, you said that: "... the SDS played a key role in the bringing down the previous authorities, as well as in the prevention of a genocide against the Serbian people by having armed it on time ..." which I read to be that you armed the Serbian people on time. Now I understand that your reference was to arming the population in general, not specifically Serbs, although that's what the speech seems to say. But what if other population, other members of the population, were armed, I take it Muslims then as well, what role could that play in the prevention of a genocide against the Serbian people? I mean, were you expecting Muslims to protect the Serbs against the genocide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were afraid that the genocide would be perpetrated precisely by the Muslims, in case conflict broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina. SDS party played a crucial role in reconciliation with the JNA. That's what I had in mind. And then they reached a decision through the Territorial Defence about the distributing the arms to the population. I meant it globally and not locally, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the fear from Serbs was a genocide committed by Muslims or -- and you would not, in order to protect the Serbs against such a genocide, arm the Muslims, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had to act according to the Territorial Defence law and its provisions, and that's what we did. In case an imminent threat of war is proclaimed, the Territorial Defence units are to receive the Territorial Defence weapons, and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I go back again to your speech, in which you say: "We armed the Serbian people in time to prevent a genocide." You explained to us now that what you meant was a general distribution of arms, not only to Serbs but to others as well, and at the same time, you tell us that the fear was that Muslims would commit such a genocide. I'm trying to reconcile the logic of your speech, the logic of what had happened, and I asked for your assistance in that. Apart from that your language seems to be clear in respect of who, under the SDS key role, who was armed in time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said here earlier on that I made a kind of global statement. Muslims in Bosnia were the majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you -- then do I have to understand your testimony to be that you made general reference to the key role of the SDS arming the Serbian people on time to prevent genocide, not specifically Prnjavor but as a wider thing that happened in some areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Is that how I have to understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I had in mind was precisely the fact that the SDS, by virtue of the fact that they supported the JNA, managed to obtain the possibility of distributing these Territorial Defence weapons and for the Serb people to be armed. But with reference to the village of Lisnja, we're not talking about any conflict, any war, because war had not broken out in Bosnia. So it was the breaking of the law and illegal arming, to a significant extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you now say, and I'm trying to reconcile that with one of your earlier answers, that the SDS was active, played an active role, in arming the Serbs. Because you said distributing these Territorial Defence weapons and for the Serb people to be armed, and that the SDS was active in that, whereas earlier you said that the SDS was never involved in any way in arming Serbs, also outside Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All that refers to political activities, and the decision to embrace the idea of the JNA as an armed force that could grant us protection, and then it was up to them to make decisions. Because those of us at the municipal level could not issue orders to the Territorial Defence. I'm talking about the political activity that led to certain orders, that led to certain events. So the Territorial Defence weapons could be distributed only on the basis of a decision that came from the Territorial Defence staff at the district level in Banja Luka. But the political mediation on the part of the SDS with regard to the JNA played a key role. That's what I had in mind; the political activity on the part of the SDS, which eventually led the army to do what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, do I then have to understand your testimony to be that the SDS politically played an active role in finally achieving arming Serbs in order to protect them against a possible genocide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of this decision, everybody was armed, but in the part of the country where we were, Serbs were in the majority, and to a significant extent, it played a role in calming the population down, in allaying their fears, since, apart from this group that came back from training in Knin, Serbs did not have any weapons. But those are rumours, and there were other rumours which are later confirmed with regard to the Muslims in Lisnja, who had more weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not an answer to my question, but, Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to be returning to the subject of Lisnja after the adjournment, but I wanted to ask you before the break about your comment, your repeated comment concerning the TO, the relationship of the municipal authorities to the TO, their ability to give orders and their relationship with them. And in that connection, let me ask you to turn quickly to tab 11, which is P529, tab 413. I know you've seen this document before, Mr. Vasic. It reflects the conclusions from the 2nd Session of the Prnjavor Crisis Staff, held on May 19th, 1992. And in particular, let me direct your attention to agenda item, or conclusion, number 8: "As regards the use of vehicles required for the needs of the Prnjavor TO, the Crisis Staff of Prnjavor Municipality hereby orders the commander of the Prnjavor TO to act in accordance with the previously adopted conclusion and to limit the use of vehicles to the necessary minimum due to difficulties in obtaining oil ..." et cetera. You told us more than once that the municipal authorities couldn't order the TO, basically were not linked to the TO, which had a vertical chain of command. How is it that on May 19th you were ordering the commander of the Prnjavor TO to do something?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This entire set of conclusions that you submitted to me means we request. Every single item begins with "we request" but not "we order." We were in charge of providing logistical support. So we can order because we don't have sufficient quantities of fuel or anything else which is necessary, and we don't want them to squander the existing resources. So it was a kind of order, because unless they acted in line with our orders, we would not be able to provide sufficient resources. We don't want the military to be driving around for no reason at all. That was that bit of the text. Perhaps it was a mistake in terms of the right expression to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in agenda item 2, you ask the TO and the chiefs of public security to prepare and submit an internal security plan so that it can be reviewed by the Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had to take care of the security of our municipality, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. since the front line in the direction of Derventa was at a distance of 30 kilometres, and we also had to take care of our own internal security and it was up to the police to do that, and we wanted them to do their job and to submit to us what they were doing so we could inform the citizens about the security situation and to let them know that we knew what the security situation within the municipality was, to what extent we were safe, since the Derventa front line was at a distance of 30 kilometres and therefore we needed internal, in-depth security within the municipality, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the effort to ensure the security of Prnjavor and the responsibility for ensuring the security of Prnjavor was discharged by close coordination and cooperation between the Crisis Staff, the municipal authorities, the TO, the police and the army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If this would be a suitable moment to have a break. Well, let me just have a look at -- we'll have a short session. No, we need a second break anyhow, so therefore we'll have a break until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I can note at this time, the Prosecution would ask for approximately five minutes at some convenient point today to address a certain procedural issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you mind -- I have to deliver a few decisions as well. It might be, since one of my colleagues has to leave, that for these practical and technical matters, such as reading decisions, and also perhaps hearing something that the other Judge could read, that we'd then sit the two of us and continue a bit at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It seems very sensible, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, let me ask you to turn your attention now to events in Lisnja. I understand that you were -- that you arrived late in the vicinity of Lisnja and were some distance from there, but I want to ask you what you might have learned subsequently, or not have learned subsequently, about events there. First of all, you indicated that both the police and the TO, including the Wolves of Vucjak, were involved in that operation; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police and the Territorial Defence participated in that operation. In the Territorial Defence, there were some 20 or 30 men, mostly the men who were on the strength of the Wolves, who at the time were under the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it's also correct that before those forces entered Lisnja, that Lisnja was shelled; isn't that right? Or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed subsequently that from a hand-held rocket launcher, three rockets were launched onto a meadow as a sign of a warning. There were no buildings there, as I was told. This was just to intimidate those who refused to return their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You don't have any personal knowledge from your own observation, do you, to dispute the testimony of any eyewitness that Lisnja was shelled?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I arrived when the operation had been well under way, and this happened towards the end of the negotiations about the return of weapons, or, as I was told, when the extremist group bust into the culture hall and seized some of those weapons that had been returned. As I've said, I arrived much later, when the operation was well under way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the answer to my question was correct; it is not necessary, although I appreciate or understand the impulse to repeat what you've said before in response to such a question, I'd appreciate it if we could move forward a little bit faster. The two mosques in the area were destroyed, and approximately 75 homes were burned down; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a lot of fires. I saw a mosque ablaze. As I've already told you, I was standing with the president of the village some 50 metres away from the mosque. Two soldiers approached us and they attempted to put the fire out. That mosque burnt down. Another mosque also burnt down. I didn't see that. That also happened during that operation. I don't know about the number of houses that were set on fire. Not all of them burnt completely. But there was a lot of damage. I'm sure you can find the number of those houses in one of the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that those mosques were primarily constructed of stone and brick and were destroyed not exclusively through fire but also by being blown up by explosives?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one that I saw had a wooden upper part, and it burnt to the ground, literally. I don't know how fire was set to it. I was never informed. We were just informed, me and the president of the village, even that the mosque was on fire, and we also saw that the upper part of the building was made of wood. We had not heard any particular explosion. There was shooting all around the place, but I can tell you that at that moment, we did not hear a detonation of any bigger explosive device. I apologise. What I'm saying is that it did not burn down to the ground; only the upper, wooden part burned completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were those mosques then, according to you, subsequently destroyed by being blown up?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was any subsequent destruction or not, but that mosque burnt. I did not stay there any longer, and I did not return to Lisnja afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the Muslim population of the area of Lisnja village was expelled; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have already testified that the Muslim population, as well as the Serbian population, had left at the beginning of the war for economic reasons. From Prnjavor, nobody left before 1995. A lot of refugees arrived in Prnjavor, and I have proof that we were the only municipality that received all those refugees. I'm talking about the Muslim refugees from Derventa. I'm sure that you will find that decision in your documentation, and I would kindly ask you if we can look at that decision. I would be very grateful to you if we could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We will turn to a decision concerning refugees shortly, but before we do, I'd like you to turn your attention, please, to tab 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, tab 12 contains P892, tab 87, and P -- excuse me. That's the only entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a secret report, military secret, top secret, strictly confidential report, from Major General Talic to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Army Main Staff, dated the 2nd of June, 1992, and in particular, Mr. Vasic, let me turn your attention to item number 2 and to the last sentence contained there, which states: "In the area of Derventa there continues to be occasional artillery fire, while because Muslim extremists have failed to hand in their weapons, the Muslim population of the area of Lisnja village has been expelled." That's in fact what happened, isn't it, precisely what General Talic reported to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see this written, but this is not correct. This is not what happened. But I'm sure that reports in the army are drafted both on verified as well as on non-verified information. I claim with full responsibility that this did not happen. A convoy was formed of some 20 or so vehicles. There were people sitting in it, men, women, and children. I approached them. I told them, "Go back to your houses, and if your house is ablaze, try to put the fire out." All the people returned on that day. On the following days -- during the following months, the population of Lisnja did not leave Lisnja, and I claim with full responsibility that this sentence is nothing but a lie, a fabrication.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How many people from Lisnja or the surrounding area ended up confined or detained in the Sloga shoe factory?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This job was carried out by the police. I am not aware of the exact number, but you have the documents and the documents tell you exactly what the number was. All those who were arrested in that operation and who were in possession of illegally obtained weapons were arrested. And if you look at the list of the weapons that were seized, you can see that it was not the Muslim members of the TO that were arrested. We're talking about M-48 rifles. There were not many of them. Maybe people had some other weapons which were kept illegally, which was a crime. I don't know any of the details. This is what I could tell from the documents. It was not up to the municipal authorities to do that job. It was the police who did it, and the judiciary afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You told us about Muslims who were arrested for possessing M-48s or other rifles. You told us about Serbs who were arrested for selling weapons to Muslims. How many Serbs were arrested for possessing an M-48 or some other rifle?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you asking me? Are you asking me about the Serbs who had sold weapons or about the Serbs who were found in possession of illegally obtained weapons or hunting rifles that they hadn't turned in? What are you asking me about? I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me change the question slightly. How many Serbian villages were attacked by Bosnian Serb forces because of suspicion that they had weapons?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the villagers returned their hunting rifles and TO weapons, save for the village of Lisnja, and the only place where the operation was carried out was the village of Lisnja. There was individual disarmament Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. on a case-by-case basis if the police station had been informed that they kept weapons. Many people failed to return their weapons, both Muslims and Serbs. And from testimony of your witness here, you could see that in 1994, the police had seized from him, from his father and from his brother, three hunting rifles. This was in 1994. They also did not obey the order, and they lived in Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You've referred on a couple of occasions to testimony before this Tribunal and to witnesses, in fact. Did you actually watch the testimony of these witnesses or were you provided with transcripts of what those witnesses had said?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw a picture of the witness on TV, and then I saw his statement among the documents when I arrived here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in your previous -- in your testimony earlier, you spoke about -- well, you spoke about Mr. Odobasic and you compared what he said in one part of his testimony to what he said in a later part his testimony. At another point in your testimony you said, about some information: "Like some witnesses claimed here." I believe that was at page 49 of yesterday's transcript. You also said: "A lot of witnesses had said that if they didn't join the army, that they were fired." That was at page 52. Since only one witness testified in this Court concerning Prnjavor, is it correct that you also watched the testimony of witnesses in the Brdjanin case or obtained the transcripts of testimony of witnesses from the Brdjanin case related to Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was some coverage on TV. Some parts of the testimonies were shown. But I received the testimonies and statements of the witnesses only here, when I arrived here. For example, I only heard of

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you also -- well, I take it you're aware that Mr. Vidic and Mr. Savic testified in the Brdjanin case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Vidic testified in the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you explain to the Court briefly who he was.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vidic was the president of the Serbian Democratic Party of the municipal board of Prnjavor, and he was also -- he was the first president of that party, and he was also a deputy in the People's Council of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You've focussed on the testimony of a number of witnesses. You were aware that Mr. Vidic said that Lisnja was ethnically cleansed, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lisnja was a Muslim village. Actually, there were two villages by the same name. There was a Serb Lisnja and a Muslim Lisnja, and the Muslim Lisnja was 100 per cent uniform Muslim village, and it could not be ethnically cleansed because it was already ethnically uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you were aware of the testimony by Mr. Vidic. You are not invited to give your own interpretation of the facts, but the question was clearly whether you are aware that Mr. Vidic said that Lisnja was ethnically cleansed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. All I know from his testimony is a two-minute clip that I saw on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were you aware that Mr. Savic, the former chief of police in Prnjavor, testified?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I hear it for the first time now from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When was Mr. Savic removed as chief of police of Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was removed -- I don't know exactly when. At the time when a few people from the Wolves of Vucjak were arrested. There had been a conflict prior to that, and I believe that the Banja Luka centre of security services found a compromise or some sort of a solution. In any case, those men were arrested, and I believe that, in their view, he was not capable of controlling the situation. And then Chief Stojan Zupljanin decided to replace Savic by Radislav Vincic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Savic disputed that, and you're aware that he has said that he was removed because he wasn't an SDS member or follower and because he didn't agree with the policy of a mono-ethnic police force?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS had an absolute power in the municipality and they could remove people or have people removed if the personnel committee and the leadership thought that that was necessary. When this was being considered, he was appointed chief. If he had not been suitable for the position, he would not have even been appointed in the first place. He was removed after having been chief of police for as long as a year and a half, although he was a Communist and his term of duty fell under the SDS leadership of the municipality. However, he was a professional and he was under the authority of the Banja Luka security services centre. And even if we had wanted to remove him, without Banja Luka, we could not have removed him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, may I ask you to answer to the question. The question was that Mr. Savic has said, and the question was whether you're aware of that, that he was removed because he wasn't an SDS member or follower and because he didn't agree with the policy of mono-ethnic police force. You have not answered that question. First of all, are you aware of that he said so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware that he said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question, then, would be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I do apologise, but we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you are not aware of it. My next question would be: Was there a policy of mono-ethnic police force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. If I may elaborate. There was a huge conflict between SDS and SDA, and we had a coalition government, even though there wasn't any need for that, but that was the political agreement that was reached, because the SDA asked for the police chief to be one of them. And we only allowed them to have the deputy commander, and we did appoint a deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that you have a different view on what happened at that time. What I'd like to -- my question to you was whether there was a mono-ethnic policy for the police force.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was, if you know, approximately the percentage of non-Serbs in the police force, let's say by mid-1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know in percentage terms, but I do know that there were at least three Croats, and this is much more than according to the population make-up throughout the war. And I'm certain that there were at least five Muslims, including the deputy commander that we ourselves appointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is to say, following our request, he was appointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was the whole of the police force? How many people, approximately? Fifty, a hundred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1991, 1992, maybe 50. And I'm talking about active police officers, the ones on active duty, not the reserve police officers. They had not even been mobilised at the time. So about 50, I would say, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did these three Croats and five Muslims remain in the police force; and if so, until when?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There were Ukrainians as well, and I think there was one Italian. And the others --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking about the five Muslims you talked about and the three Croats, so let's leave alone the Ukrainians and the Italians. Did they remain --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All these indications are approximate numbers, because this was not within my area of competence. But I do know as a citizen. I believe that the Croats stayed until the end, until the end of the war, all of them. And as to Muslims, I think they stayed until 1992. After 1992, I don't think there were any left in the police force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would you have any idea when in 1992? Because that covers 12 months. Mid-1992, early 1992, autumn 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The end of 1992, I believe in the fall of 1992. I think they received the instructions from their party to leave this institution. I mean their party, the SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They voluntarily left on their own, without any -- no one was fired, no one was -- I'm just trying to find out. So they all went because they wanted to leave the police force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I might go wrong if I try to give you a specific answer, because I'm not sure. Perhaps they were not particularly keen to be members of the police force. I can't give you a specific answer because I might go wrong there and I'm not sure. I know they were not fired. That I do know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if you don't know, please tell us, because it's of no use to hear any evidence unless the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the exact answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We were talking about events in Lisnja. You had an opportunity to look at General Talic's report of June 2nd. If we can turn to the next tab number. That would be tab number 13. That's a report by General Talic on the following day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would need an exhibit number, I take it, Mr. Tieger, because we have an exhibit number, but only in Brdjanin, isn't it? At least --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is correct, at least as our records indicate.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 13, Your Honour, will be given Prosecution Exhibit number P948, and the English translation will be P948.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Vasic, this is a report by General Talic to the VRS Main Staff. Directing your attention to item number 2, the last sentence indicates: "Measures have been taken to continue -" "ciscenje" in the B/C/S - "the areas of Kozarac, Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc, and Lisnja [as read] village near Prnjavor." So it's correct, is it not, that here General Talic is reporting that this same activity is being pursued in Kozarac, Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kljuc, are being pursued by the army in Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I set eyes on this, and I think it is a lie, pure and simple. And as far as I know, nothing could have happened there without my knowing or having heard of it. I don't know what kind of cleansing he meant. Probably ethnic cleansing. He didn't say it in so many words. But I can claim upon my full responsibility this never happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I indicated earlier I wanted to turn to various ways of -- or various activities that might have been involved in the departure of Muslims from Prnjavor, but you asked if we could turn to decisions by the Crisis Staff concerning refugees, and in that connection I'd like to direct your attention to a portion of the document that I think is contained in your materials, and that's a decision of the Crisis Staff from June 22nd, 1992. If you look at the portions of the gazette that you provided, I think it's contained at item number 42. Do you see that, Mr. Vasic, "Decision on an organised moving out of refugees"?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't found it yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What tab are we? It's the material that was used yesterday or --?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you'll give me one moment to consult with my case manager. This is not in the binder, I know that, or I believe that's the case. But I think it's available for distribution. If not, I'll have the translation placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If that's the decision, number 42, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, we can distribute the English -- no? I guess we have to place it on the ELMO, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do not know where to find it in the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's page 9 of these reports, yes. And of course we'll supplement the binder, Your Honour, with the appropriate English translation copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to go to private session just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I take you back to an earlier portion of your testimony, which was about -- we're not in private session yet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have to ask the public gallery to be ... It might not take very long. We are not in private session yet?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, you were looking at a decision found at item number 42 that was taken on June 19th, 1992 and apparently adopted or signed on June 22nd, 1992, a translation of which appears on the ELMO. This is a decision on an organised moving out of refugees disloyal to the authorities of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Article 1 states that: "All refugees currently residing in the area of Prnjavor municipality who are disloyal to the authorities of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as the refugees whose relatives are members of enemy formations, are obliged to leave the area of Prnjavor municipality in an organised fashion, and in compliance with the regulations in force in the area of the municipality." Was this the decision related to refugees that you wanted to bring the Court's attention to?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision refers only and exclusively to the Serb refugees.
