At that moment, we had 9.000 refugees from Western Slavonia, and many were disloyal in the sense that they did not comply with the law according to which all persons between 18 or 60 years of age - all males, that is to say - either had to be in the army or to do the so-called work duty, to work in companies, et cetera. And there were quite a few people who didn't want to do either, and they were a huge financial burden, and we felt that this was disloyal behaviour. And we thus gave them the opportunity to go somewhere else, where maybe such behaviour would have been tolerated. And because of rumours that reached us, according to which some Serb man's parents, for example, reached Prnjavor as refugees, and their son remained -- and was still serving in the Croat armed forces. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. In order to avoid any difficulties, we felt it would have been better for them to go somewhere else and not stay in our municipality. And this is a decision that referred to Serb refugees only, because the only refugees we had at the time were Serbs. And I wanted to draw the attention to other refugees, the Muslims, and that's the second decision, if you want to put it on the ELMO maybe. This is the second decision I'm referring to now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first seek a clarification. You said it was just Serb refugees because "the only refugees we had at the time were Serbs." Was that before the refugees from - I think you told us from Derventa - the Muslim refugees, arrived in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Muslims, refugees from Derventa, stayed in Prnjavor for about nine to ten hours, and this decision that I tried to refer to earlier on was about the Muslims from Derventa. Since we, that is to say I myself, when I was informed that they would like to come and stay at the municipality of Prnjavor, I took the initiative and decided that they should be allowed to come. And in the meantime, I had organised a Crisis Staff meeting and the decision was made in line with what is indicated here. We had talks with the representatives of the Muslim people, and they were not willing to accept these refugees for economic reasons. They were afraid that they wouldn't be able to have them for a long time, or maybe for some other reasons as well. And in the afternoon, escorted by a police car, and in order to make sure that they should travel safely, I travelled in that police car, and then they were taken to Tesanj and were allowed to cross over into the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But I would have liked you to take a look at that decision, because in one instance it says, literally, that elderly men, if they -- or rather, older men, if they wished to do so, could either join the Republika Srpska army or else they could do the so-called work duty. And it transpires very clearly from this decision that whoever didn't wish to join the army didn't have to do so. It was not a coercive measure. And I've had quite a few problems because of this decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether you're going to pay any attention to the other decision. We'd like to see it. I don't know whether you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe the Court does have it. It's not -- and if not, we'll provide it. But I think it's in the materials. The witness has addressed it. In the interests of time, I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just want to clarify one issue, Mr. Vasic, in connection with the events at Lisnja and the forces involved. And in that regard, I would ask you to turn to tab 14, which contains P749, tab 3. This is an order dated 5 June 1992, by General Talic. And in item number 1 it states that: "The battalion from the Prnjavor Territorial Defence Command on Mount Vucjak is hereby transferred to the command of the 327th Motorised Brigade and fully incorporated into it." First of all, the battalion from -- the Prnjavor TO on Mount Vucjak refers to the Wolves of Vucjak; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This popular name is the Wolves from Vucjak, but they were always incorporated within a unit, and officially they were a part of that unit. But amongst themselves, they used to call one another Wolves from Vucjak, and you can see General Talic addressed them in that way as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. And here in Court we've been referring to the Wolves of Vucjak. I just want you to confirm that the reference here to the battalion from the Prnjavor Territorial Defence command on Mount Vucjak is a reference to that group.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as we can see in item 2, Veljko Milankovic is appointed as battalion commander by General Talic, and as a result of his transfer and full incorporation into the 327th Motorised Brigade, will carry out and receive orders from the commander of that brigade. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So prior to General Talic's order of June 5th, the Wolves of Vucjak were part of the Prnjavor Territorial Defence command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a period when they depended on the previous commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, and they were actually incorporated into a Banja Luka unit which was in Western Slavonia, in Jasenovac. The colonel, or the general, as he was later, was General Uzelac. This is something I mentioned before. They were always assigned to a unit. They were always within a Banja Luka unit at the orders of General Uzelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is quite clear. Mr. Tieger wants to know whether the Wolves were, previous to that appointment, were in a TO unit from Prnjavor, not whether they were in a Banja Luka. Just whether they were -- and I looked yesterday at the document of I think the sub-commander, the name was missing, where I think twice it appears that at least this member of this unit, this sub-commander, was in the TO Prnjavor, isn't it? I mean, that's what Mr. Tieger asks you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously, you don't understand that the 1st Krajina Corps used this unit all this time and shifted it from one unit to another. And the Territorial Defence was under the command of the army, and the army could use any unit of the Territorial Defence wherever and whenever they wanted. And that's what they did with the Wolves as well. For example, they would send them to one part of the front line for ten days and then to another part for ten days. And the Territorial Defence was not under our command; it was under the command of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one asked you about the command. The only question was whether the Wolves were part of the Prnjavor Territorial Defence previous to this decision. That's the only thing. You were asked about facts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please, next time, just say yes to the clear question of Mr. Tieger. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How closely did you coordinate with Veljko Milankovic or any other members of the Prnjavor TO before their operation in Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day when this would be done, the strategy, the tactics, none of this I was informed about. This was agreed between the police and the army. I didn't even know which unit would be engaged on behalf of the army, or which part of which unit would be engaged in that operation. I tried to be close to Veljko privately, in order to be able to control the situation when it came to a certain problem in Prnjavor, and I tried to be as close to all the other commanders. If, for example, any of their men were responsible for any of the problems, that gave me an opportunity to control that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you talk to Milankovic after the operation in Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I indicated to you that I wanted to return at some point to the factors involved in the departure of Muslims from Prnjavor. We talked earlier about the impact of discriminatory acts or harassment. I take it you would agree that being subjected to discriminatory conduct and to beatings by the police would be a factor in encouraging people to leave the municipality.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. What is it that you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Beatings or physical abuse by law enforcement representatives of a municipality would encourage the members of any nationality subjected to such conduct to leave the municipality, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the Chamber wonders whether this is not self-explanatory and whether it might not be more important to see whether such a thing happened, rather than what the results would be. It goes without much explanation, I take it, that you would agree with that, Mr. Josse, as well; that if you would be beaten up by the police officers, that this would certainly not encourage to stay close to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please, let's please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think the witness may have been having some conceptual difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Muslims in Prnjavor were taken into custody, were interrogated by police and were beaten by police, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police did what they were supposed to do. All those who did something against the law were brought in. The police were independent. Whether they overstepped their authority or not, I can't be the judge of that. But in any case, this doesn't happen on a large scale. And this is what I claim, that this never happened on a large scale. I spoke to the chief of police very often, and he would tell me what was going on in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you inspect police facilities or areas -- or locations where Muslims were detained?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of any Muslim in Prnjavor being detained. There's no detention facility in Prnjavor. I only know that across the road from the school, in the Sloga factory building, after the operation in Lisnja, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. while they were being interviewed, these people were kept, and then they were released after having been interviewed. I never inspected them. This was the job of the police and the court. They were all interviewed, they were all sentenced. The judge was a lady from a mixed marriage; one of their parents was a Croat and the other Montenegrin. The lady who kept a record was a Croatian. That's what I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you about another way of encouraging Muslims to leave the area or letting them know that they were not welcome in the area. You referred to the departure of Muslims in 1995. Would you agree - and perhaps this is another self-evident question, and if so, I apologise and will withdraw it - that refusing people permission to bury their dead is one method calculated to get people to leave the municipality?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was never the case. There was never a ban on burials, either of Muslims or any other ethnic group. There is a decision which was the product of the zoning regulation of the town preceding the war. According to that decision, the Muslim cemetery, which is in the centre of the town, some ten metres away from the hotel, should have been conserved and there should have been a joint cemetery for Croats, Serbs, and Muslims, in the same place where the cemetery for Croats and Serb cemetery had already existed. And part of that cemetery was to be designated for the Muslim population. This is on the outskirts of the city. This decision was the product of previous discussions on the zoning regulation. This decision was issued in 1994. If the goal had been different, it would have been issued in 1991. This decision is still in effect, but it has never been implemented. However, it has never been made null and void either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's break that down slightly. First of all, the decision you're referring to was one that you signed; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we have a copy of that decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, you'll find that at tab 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It needs a new number. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be P949, and the English translation will be P949.1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that decision, Mr. Vasic, refers to the Muslim cemetery in Prnjavor, does it not?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision applies to the Muslim cemetery, the only one that existed in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you were aware, were you not, that in subsequent decisions, one dated on 30 August 1998, found at tab 28, and one dated 23 November 1999, found at tab 29 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'll ask for a number on that in a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- that a Muslim resident of Prnjavor was ordered to dig up his wife's body and remove it from that cemetery because it had been buried without permission. And the Islamic community of Prnjavor was forbidden to bury a particular deceased member of the community in that cemetery, both in response to your decision of 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that this decision is still in force, but it has never been implemented. My decision from 1994 was based on the law on zoning regulation. I still believe that this decision should be implemented, that the town -- the cemetery in the town should be conserved, which is a normal thing in any civilised, urban area, and that the new cemetery should be used, as provided for by the decision. These two documents were issued when I was no longer an official in the municipality. The decision that I issued, that the municipality issued, has not been respected, which means the people who do that actually break the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm wondering: We do see a decision where -- it's stated that the burial of the dead shall take place at the new town cemetery located somewhere else. Is it the position of the Prosecutor that if in violation of such a rule, you bury someone, that you should leave the deceased's body in the place where it should not have been buried? And I don't know the other decision, 29, but is it the position of the Prosecution that if 5, 6 years later, someone wants to bury a deceased relative on a cemetery which has been closed in 1994, that that should be -- that it is any expression of discriminatory acts? I have to understand -- I have some difficulty understanding exactly the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's because if, with all respect, the point is not completed yet, and I think it will -- at least the Prosecution's position will be made clear both with the next document and with the next few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's wait. Please proceed, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Vasic, this decision was taken before the human rights chamber in Bosnia and Herzegovina, was it not?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which decision was taken before the human rights chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of background questions, then. First of all, the decision that you made in 1994 didn't affect the nearby Orthodox or Catholic cemeteries; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did indirectly, because in the second part of the decision, we said that people should be buried in the eastern part of the town, in the Catholic and Orthodox cemetery, where, according to the zoning regulation, this should have been the cemetery for all three peoples. The experts for zoning decided that this should be the location of all the three cemeteries. Nobody wanted to touch the existing Muslim cemetery, like this witness said that we decided to build something there and that we -- that this was a sacrilege. And I claim with full responsibility that there were no construction sites ever. There have never been any construction works taking place on that Muslim cemetery in the town. This cemetery should have been conserved. That was the idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One more point before I turn to the decision itself. There was no shortage of space in that cemetery. There was enough space in that cemetery to accommodate Muslim burials for the next 50 years; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not down to the space, but the expert opinion of the people who were in charge of the zoning regulation during the war -- or before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was it -- is it correct that there was more than sufficient space in that cemetery and space enough to bury deceased people for decades, irrespective of anything else you want to tell us? Let's just get an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That is correct. I don't know whether this would last for decades, but in any case, there was still enough space.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you to turn to tab 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we perhaps assign the numbers first to 28, 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 28 would be --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P950, Your Honours, with the English translation, P950.1. And tab 29 would be given P951, with the English translation P951.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, tab 30 contains a decision on admissibility and merits in a case entitled "The Islamic community in Bosnia and Herzegovina against the Republika Srpska." And that's a decision, as you can see, which bears on the issue we've been discussing, the Muslim town cemetery in Prnjavor. I'm going to direct your attention to certain aspects, certain findings by the Court. First of all, in paragraph number 14, the Court indicates that the facts of the dispute are essentially not in dispute. In paragraph 18, the Court indicates that the new town cemetery in the eastern part of town does not exist as of the date of that decision in the year 2000. And if you'll turn, finally, in the interests of time --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He needs to read it, Your Honour. He needs to read number 18, at the very least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's give an opportunity to the witness to read 18.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have had an opportunity to see these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you are familiar with the relevant portions. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I can turn you to essentially the concluding findings of the document at paragraphs 104 and 105. The chamber made the following finding, noting first that: "... the ordinance affected only the Muslim cemetery and not the Orthodox or Catholic cemeteries situated nearby, and that there was no shortage of space for burials in the Muslim cemetery, the space available being sufficient for the next 50 years." And then in paragraph 105: "In the circumstances, the chamber finds the applicant's suggestion that the purpose of the continued enforcement of the 1994 ordinance is to discourage the return of Bosniak refugees and displaced persons to Prnjavor by preventing them from freely pursuing their religious traditions has not been seriously challenged and is the only plausible explanation of that decision. The continued closure Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the cemetery, under an ordinance adopted in pursuance of a policy of ethnic cleansing, involves differential treatment of Muslims and cannot be regarded as pursuing any legitimate aim." Were you aware that after full litigation of this matter, the Court was unable to find any plausible explanation for the ordinance other than that it was adopted pursuant to a policy of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision was adopted -- or this ordinance was adopted in keeping with the law. And as I know, the municipality of Prnjavor appealed against this decision, and what it says here, that the cemetery doesn't exist, is not correct. There is a cemetery. There has been a cemetery for a long time. There is a place for the cemetery. It is true that there was enough space, but when this decision was being issued, this was not an issue. The space was not an issue. It was an issue of zoning. We wanted to have the cemetery in the town conserved and that all new burials would take place in a new cemetery some 500 metres away from the old cemetery, outside of the town. I don't know what other intentions were. I don't want to speculate. I don't want anybody else to speculate. These were not our intentions. If those had been our intentions, we would have issued the ordinance in 1991, not in 1994. And again I repeat: The ordinance was issued based on the discussions that took place before the war, when the Muslim was the president of the municipality, when the party of -- League of Communists was in power. So that's when the discussions took place, and the ordinance was issued based on those discussions, and the intention was to have a joint cemetery outside of the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasic, you said a few things. You said that the decision, where it says that the cemetery doesn't exist, is not correct. The next sentence was: "There is a cemetery." Then you said: "There has been a cemetery for a long time." Then you say: "There is a place for the cemetery." And then, a few lines later, you say: "We --" you're talking about a new cemetery some 500 metres away from the old cemetery. So you said there was a cemetery, there is a cemetery, the decision is wrong, and there was supposed to be a new cemetery. I have some -- I would like to fully understand your testimony in this respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept that I might have confused the issue a bit. The facts are very clear, however. In Prnjavor, there is a Muslim cemetery, which is the subject of this decision, and there is also a cemetery where, up to then, and even today, Serbs and Croats have been buried. And there is also a plot of land where this second cemetery can be extended to. When I said "new cemetery," I meant a new cemetery for the Muslims. But it is one and the same thing. It is the already existing cemetery for the Croats and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has this extension been realised? You said there was a plot available next to the Croat and Serbian cemetery which would be available. Has this been, well, prepared as a cemetery, by putting walls, by putting -- whatever way is this plan you had, is it realised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the zoning regulation, this plot of the land next to the cemetery has been envisaged for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And my question was not whether place has been reserved to create such a separate part of a larger cemetery specific for Muslims, but whether this has been realised by either putting a wall, putting gates, making a path. That's the way how you create a cemetery. Has this been done or is it just that it has been envisaged by the planning authority that it could be done there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You would have to allow me two sentences in order to elaborate and explain. You don't have to, but I would kindly ask you to allow me the two sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If they are part of an answer to my question, I will allow it, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, not a single cemetery is properly tended and organised; not the Muslim, not the Orthodox, not the Catholic ones, so we don't have proper paths and et cetera. This is just an area where people get buried. And even today it's like that, unfortunately. But you know what plot of land is for what group. I don't know what the term is it; tradition maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there's more needed to make a plot of land a cemetery. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I have some insight into the Court's schedule?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Not only the schedule, but I have to confront you that you're at least 60 per cent, approximately, for the cross-examination. So therefore, let me just see. We are 20 minutes off from 10 minutes to 1.00. Let's first look at the technical side of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The technicians could go on for another 20 minutes, but I'm also asking the interpreters. Then we have 20 minutes left. Mr. Tieger, you know that the Defence always insists that the 60 per cent is not a rule but a guidance, but just as good a guidance for the Prosecution as for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm trying to follow that, Your Honour, but I will not make it on this occasion. There is still a considerable number of documents to cover. I will say again that, with additional time to address -- to locate, address these materials, the examination might have been expedited to some extent. We had considerable difficulty arising from the belated receipt of the exhibits. I'm not going to suggest that there aren't ways in which to otherwise expedite the examination, but on this occasion, I am asking the Court's understanding and latitude and the opportunity to present the Court with the documents that we have found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would necessarily mean that the witness would have to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. I think that's regrettable, but it's certainly not, unfortunately, the first time that's happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, any observations in respect of what Mr. Tieger has asked for?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, I don't think I've got any observations in relation to that. Could I, Your Honour, briefly throw one other matter into Your Honour's scales, and that's simply this: In reliance of the Chamber rising at 12.45 today, I need to be out of here by, at the very latest, 1.30, the very latest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that would not be a problem, because we could not continue anyhow. I mean, this Chamber is, unless -- apart from reading decisions, which is a totally different matter than hearing evidence, we'd prefer to hear it all three of us. And certainly since -- let's just see. How much time would you still need, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I mean, Your Honour, I want to make it clear, we're not going to finish today. How much time after that, if I were to continue today, it would clearly be longer than if I -- in other words, my estimate for concluding today would be longer than the time it will take when I have a greater chance to review and refine the materials. I suspect that I'd be able to conclude in roughly one session; that is, not a full day, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're just considering the possibilities. Mr. Josse, I do understand that you have to leave, and we scheduled -- we know that tomorrow might be a day which you prefer not to work. Are you going to leave The Hague, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Friday is beyond you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going back to London for the holiday, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And then I'm going to Bosnia on Friday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that gives no way out for Friday. And today you say you have to leave at 1.30?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I do, I'm afraid, because, A, I've got a flight booked, but B, the reason I had to catch the flight at that time was in order to celebrate the holiday in the appropriate manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. And if you would get any additional support in transportation or something like that which would -- I mean, I usually take my time not to miss my flight, but sometimes if transportation is made more easy to me, then I usually take a bit less time. I don't know -- for example, if I would go by train to Schiphol airport, I would know what time it would take me. If my wife would bring it me, it would take a bit more; if my son would drive me, it would take a bit less.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to take public transport there, but I suppose I could look into making other arrangements or Mr. Karganovic could on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That all doesn't make any sense at all if we could not finish today. I mean, then it's really useless. Up until now, Mr. Josse, could you give us an estimate on, as matters stand now, how much time you would need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Bearing I mind I thought the witness had to leave today, I was going to ask him one question, effectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I suspect, and given the opportunity, I might spend a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. little bit longer on the subject. But I'd rather he had the opportunity to go home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And not come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's, of course, a balance you'll have to make. Mr. Tieger, looking at the clock and taking into consideration that the Bench would be willing even to change its commitments elsewhere, if you would have, well, let's say another 35 minutes, would you be able to finish in that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour, to be perfectly honest. And I would love to say otherwise, but I don't think that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we would impose on you to do it in 40 or 45 minutes, could we then at the end see whether there would be an urgent need to have the witness recalled?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm obviously at the Court's disposal for that. I'm more than prepared to do my best, but I don't want to mislead the Court into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. But of course I just ask you to at least to prioritise as much as you can for the next 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I've just been doing that and considering also potential technical difficulties, and there are at least one video, there's an intercept. I'm pessimistic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another question would be how much time would we need for the change of tapes? Because we could not continue until a further break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Finally, another 20 minutes would be taken by changing the tapes, so that would reduce the time to such that we could not continue. Mr. Tieger, we'll follow the schedule as before. We'll later see -- since you had one question in mind, then we'll have to consider what to do at a later stage, Mr. Josse. I don't know whether this is a question which is the kind of simple one-line question, but -- which could be put -- questions like, "Have you testified to the best of your ability?" I mean, these are the kind of questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me make it clear. If Your Honour is going to cut this cross-examination short, I'm prepared not to re-examine the witness, not because I don't want him to be properly cross-examined, but because I'd like him to have the opportunity to go home and not have to come back, which will clearly be very onerous on him. So I will ask no questions, on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can't give any promise on that basis. Mr. Tieger, you can proceed and let's see how far we come until close to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I want to turn to some of the decisions made by the Prnjavor Crisis Staff, and I want to look first, if we can, at the decision which, as you indicated, prompted the disarming efforts and ultimately the events in Lisnja, and that's the 4 May decision. And I believe that's found at tab 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is P237, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, earlier we looked at the decision by the Prnjavor Crisis Staff that referred to a decision by the ARK Crisis Staff, which was number 01-1/92, dated May 4, 1992. I take it you remember that reference in the Prnjavor Crisis Staff decision, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So now we have before us that decision by the ARK Crisis Staff which indicates that it was pursuant to the decision of the Ministry of the National Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, dated 16 April 1992. I'd like to turn to a subsequent decision by the ARK Crisis Staff, found at tab 10. That's a decision dated 11 May 1992, which needs a new number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. That will need to be assigned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The number will be given soon. Mr. Registrar is doing something else on my request. So the number will be attached to tab 10. Tab 30, we need a number anyhow as well, so let me try to take over. Tab 29 was 951, tab 30 is 952, and tab 10 will be 953.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, the decision of 11 May 1992 extends the deadline for surrender of illegally acquired weapons and also indicates that: "After the expiration of that deadline ... the most severe sanctions will be taken against those that disobey the proclamation of the Crisis Staff." Do you know, sir, whether the deadline was extended beyond May 14th or whether that was the operative date for Prnjavor and the other municipalities in the area?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether it was extended. Since there are no other conclusions, probably not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm trying to adjust so we don't find ourselves in the middle of a topic when the end of the session hits, so I'm going to turn to another subject, if I may, at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll continue for another 10 to 12 minutes, but that's the bare limit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, you indicated, I believe, some of the efforts that you've made prior to coming to Court to obtain information from various sources and some of your proactive efforts to acquire that information; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are there other steps that you took that you didn't detail to the Court to get information to bring to the Court?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in what sense you mean. I tried to talk to people who used to work with me at the time, in order to jog my memory, because quite some time has passed, so I think I've forgotten quite a few things as well. And I had a long talk with the president of the executive committee, Radivoje Radivojevic, who was in charge of a number of these decisions, as the president of the executive committee, because I didn't have my private archives where I could keep all those documents. And after 12 or 13 years, it is a bit difficult to recall everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you've indicated to the Court on a number of occasions that your motivation for doing so was to obtain as much information as possible to present objectively to the Court.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To get as much information as possible in order to be able to prove before this Court that there was no ethnic cleansing and that there were no crimes in Prnjavor, the crimes that the accused is accused of. And it can be confirmed, even today, very often both in the Federation and the Republika Srpska, people keep referring to us as those who actually managed to set a good example of how things should be done, under such difficult conditions, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for clarity's sake, there's nothing you're expected here to prove. You're just expected to give answers to the best of your knowledge to the questions put to you. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, it would be fair to say, wouldn't it, that at least part of your motivation springs from the fact that you are a long-time and devoted follower of Dr. Karadzic and of Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My motivation was to try and prove that the unfair and unjust accusations referred to by this particular witness are untrue, and I would be very sorry if the accused were to be held responsible for this part of the indictment, because what is being said here, that is to say, blaming certain facts in the municipality of Prnjavor on Mr. Krajisnik, that's just incorrect. I mean, I had a choice as to whether I wanted to give evidence or not, but I consented to give evidence because this is simply not true. And I'm trying to protect the municipality of Prnjavor's good name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But it is correct, isn't it, that you are a long-time and indeed devoted follower of -- well, let's start with Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ideas advocated by the SDS party, headed by Dr. Karadzic, yes, I embraced those ideas and I'm still a member of the Serb Democratic Party even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Not just the ideas, but the man as well. You've supported him and continue to support him, don't you?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I value those men. If there is something that they did, and I'm not aware of it, in that case, I'm wrong. And as to the facts that I'm aware of, I hold him in high esteem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. Perhaps I should complement this. I was a local politician. I was not the president of the party or a member of parliament, so I didn't know enough about these global issues, other than the information that was given to us. According to my knowledge, I'm not aware of them having perpetrated these things. But for a while, we were separated physically, in terms of territories, as to whether other things were going on in Serb Sarajevo or where they were, I do not know and I can't testify to that. And during the war, I went to Sarajevo only very, very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure you knew I'd ask about this, but you were dismissed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. from your position as manager of the Republika Srpska Roads Directorate last year by the High Representatives for your participation in, according to the High Commissioner, in fostering a culture of silence and deceit, wherein war crime indictees are protected from justice; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NEMANJA VASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For four years, I was the director of the Roads Directorate of the Republika Srpska, and on the 25th of June, the public competition was published again, because it was the end of my mandate. I had the best recommendations and references from the World Bank in Washington and that's why I was elected again, and I got so much praise that I couldn't even recognise myself. But six days later, I was removed, together with other 59 men, but the rationale was not the one that you're referring to, but it said it was because I was holding a position which would make it possible for me to assist and abet indicted war criminals and that I was doing so. But it is incorrect, and there's no proof of that, and I'm not in a position to do that. Because since 1997, I have never had any idea of the whereabouts of Radovan Karadzic, who is a war crimes indictee. And I am expecting to be reinstated very shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a copy of that decision available for the Chamber? Is it in the tabs?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is not in the tabs, and I apologise for that. We'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because if the decision is not there, we would have to rely on the witness who said what is in the decision, and especially if there are any written documents, the Chamber prefers to directly be able to read the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I quite agree, and we will certainly get the full text of the decision, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not unless it's put to the witness, I submit. It needs to be put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, the witness, I hardly could expect the decision not to be known to the witness. But of course there could be different versions, but that's a rather --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do know about it. I received a copy of that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I expect under those circumstances, Mr. Josse. Mr. Tieger, we are close to 1.00. On this subject, if you would have one or two more questions, you could put them to the witness. Otherwise we'll stop at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm at the Court's disposal, Your Honour. I wouldn't want to run over, and we are getting close to a video, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I do have one -- there's one area I could explore with him. It involves a document. It's tab -- I'm at the Court's disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have another matter on the agenda. Mr. Vasic, the Chamber regrets that we're not today in a position, because the Chamber itself might have some questions for you as well, we're not in a position to finish your examination. Could you return, and when could you return? This Court will not sit until the 25th. Would there be any possibility -- of course I'm also looking at you, Mr. Josse, whether the 25th would be the right time or somewhat after that. I can imagine that you made arrangements already.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'd be happy for him to return -- I see Mr. Harmon laughing. I'd be happy for him to return on the 25th, Your Honour. If he is able to. I mean, clearly we're going to need another witness here that day, and I know it's something Mr. Harmon wishes to address with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vasic, would there be a possibility for you to be back in this courtroom on the 25th of October? As I said, I regret that we have to ask you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Considering the reason why I'm here, I'm going to come back on the 25th, although I would have preferred to have finished today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the Chamber would have preferred as well. You'll get further information from the Victims and Witnesses Section. We'd like to continue on the 25th with this witness. That would be in Courtroom II, and also at 9.00 in the morning. The Victims and Witnesses Section will give you further information. Meanwhile, you're supposed not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given and you're still about to give, and that's perhaps even more difficult to do that if you're away for a considerable period of time, but nevertheless, that's how you are instructed to behave. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We're going to need a limited amount of communication with him through a -- we'll do it through the Victims and Witnesses Section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For practicalities, I take it also for the Prosecution that's accepted. We have to stop -- yes. The witness is excused, can leave the courtroom, preferably leaving all the Court documents in here. Thank you very much also for coming back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we have problems with the tapes. The Chamber suggests, since Mr. Josse told us that he would have to leave not later than 1.30, to have a break as short as possible, if everyone would be standby, well, let's say after 17 or 18 minutes, so that we -- usually we're told that 20 minutes is the minimum. But let's try to start immediately. We could then deal with the procedural issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any time left before Mr. Josse leaves, I'd also like to read out two decisions. We'll stand adjourned for as short as possible, and we'll restart certainly not later than 20 minutes past 1.00. --- Break taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It might not surprise the parties that I have to announce that Judge Hanoteau is, for urgent reasons, absent. We'll only deal with procedural matters at this moment. Mr. Josse, in view of the time, did I understand well that you thought that you could delay your observations on the problems you discussed earlier in private session until we resume after the ten days' break?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That would be ideal, from my point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll then hear from you. Any issue, procedural issue, to be raised by the Prosecution at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is. I have raised this with Mr. Josse yesterday in an e-mail, I raised it this morning in the first recess, we had a conversation about it. The problem is this: We have struggled mightily with the late disclosure of a proper 65 ter summary and the identification of a witness, and even more difficult for us was the late receipt of documents, untranslated, that made our preparations almost impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fully understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So the reason I bring this to Your Honours' attention: We will be starting court again in 13 days. I yesterday sent Mr. Josse an e-mail asking to have the identification of the next witness and a 65 ter summary and copies of the exhibits, and could he inform me as to when. I just inform the Court that we have not received that. I know Mr. Josse and I talked and he was prepared to make submissions on that, but we have not received that, and I don't want to repeat the difficulties that we had on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, could you give us any idea on when you think you could disclose the summary, 65 ter summary, the updated one, and a list of exhibits for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I'm being honest, not really. Yesterday we had a meeting, and we set in train a system to try and, as best we can, to alleviate this problem. And Mr. Karganovic and another B/C/S speaker on our team are going to work on this immediately. It's an absolute priority for them, of course, and they'll be able to liaise with me. But realistically, we won't know the name of the witness, I wouldn't have thought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would have thought at least 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 48 hours means that -- I do understand that you'll travel Friday to Bosnia, and I take it that you'll meet some persons, and that by Friday you could --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That is part of the idea, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we've set in train some efforts to try and get the exhibits at least to me, and if they can get to me, then I can get them here, so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just say, it is a desperately unsatisfactory situation, and I can only apologise to my learned friends and their staff. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me cut this short. I am a bit aware of your programme of the days to come. I do understand that tomorrow is not a working day for you. Friday you'll travel to Bosnia. From Friday on, although I'll not be in the country, I want to be kept informed on a day-by-day basis on any developments in this respect. That means that by Friday I want to be kept informed whether you have already identified the next witness, how many exhibits you expect to use, and if you don't know yet, how many you have identified up until that moment, whether you did send it by fax to the Prosecution. I want to be kept informed on a day-by-day basis on every single progress made in this respect. Because, as you said, and of course I could hear from you how unacceptable it is and how much you regret it, that I can imagine what you'd like to say, and I've heard it already several times. The thing now is what we have to do. For the first witness it went not the way it should have gone, that is, exhibits just the day before, approximately. The next witness should show a huge improvement. That means even if we -- and we can't meet the two weeks' deadline, it should at least be far better than the first one. I also take it, Mr. Josse, that when you're travelling in Bosnia, that you would also prepare for the next witnesses to come. So I want for every following witness, I want an improvement of the performance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's the idea, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. It's, however, a bit late to start creating processes for this at this very moment. But let's not -- let me not be -- let me try not to focus on criticising you, but let me focus extremely on the improvement of the present situation. Anything else to be said about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Nothing, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The way in which you'll communicate with me when I'm not in The Hague, you'll be informed about that. Then any other procedural issue to be raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Josse, I'm looking at the clock. You said you had to leave not later --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I mention something about what the Court is about to do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is a rather bizarre request. If the Court is about to find in the Defence's favour on the certification for the 98 bis, could I ask that not be done today? Because that will then cause a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be in favour, yes. Well, to be quite honest to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If it's against --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You might be shocked by it, but the decisions are there, but are not in favour of a certification.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Then they can be given now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I have the following: I have one decision on Zvornik contextual exhibits, which is a relatively short one. Then I have two decisions to be read. Keeping in mind, Mr. Josse, that you'd like not to miss your plane, one of the practical ways of doing it would be that if you'd say, "I'd rather leave, but if the Chamber would have a copy for its own use for these decisions, let me rather catch my plane and read it on my way to the plane," because there will be no opportunity for you anyhow to discuss it with Mr. Krajisnik any more, then exceptionally, the Chamber would provide you with the text I've got in front of me and which I'll read at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That would be desirable from my personal point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then I'll just first read the decision on Zvornik contextual exhibits, then I'll give you the decision which I'm about to read on the other matters and leave you a copy of that. I start with the admittance of Zvornik contextual exhibits. I take it that it's distributed to the transcribers and to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not. Well, it was available, so I'm a bit surprised that it's not. I'll start reading very slowly. On the 12th of July, the final version of the Zvornik contextual exhibits was tendered. The Defence did not object to the admission of any of these exhibits. The Chamber admitted the exhibits as a package, together with a large number of other exhibits, on the 19th of July. However, the Chamber kept one particular exhibit, the witness statement made by Branko Studen on the 11th of July, under further consideration. If the Prosecution wishes to have such a witness statement given to the Prosecution team in 2003 admitted into evidence, it should, in principle, follow the Rule set out for admission of these witness statements, namely, Rule 92 bis. The statement of Branko Studen tendered by the Prosecution cannot, therefore, be admitted into evidence as a contextual exhibit. Noting that in the index to the Zvornik contextual package, the Prosecution has called Branko Studen's statement a Rule 68 statement, which we understand to be an exculpatory statement, the Chamber recalls that any material the Prosecutor deems to fall under Rule 68 should be disclosed to the Defence and the Defence may then decide whether it does in fact consider the material to be exculpatory and whether or not it wishes to tender the material into evidence. This concludes the decision of the Chamber regarding the admittance of the Zvornik contextual exhibits. Then the two decisions I'll read out, Mr. Josse. The first one is you were asking for an extension of time to apply for certification to appeal the Chamber's decision on the motion for acquittal, and an application for certification is attached to the extension of time application. Extension of time is denied, which of course also means that the application for certification is implicitly denied. Nevertheless, the Chamber gives some reasons why it would have denied that motion as well, even if the extension of time would have been granted. Then the other decision is the application for a certificate to appeal the Chamber's denial of the Defence motion for extension of time in which to comply with the Rule 65 ter (G) requirements, and that motion is -- that application for a certificate is denied as well. You can be provided with a copy of the reasons so you can read it for yourself. I'll read it out now in Court and then we'll adjourn until the 25th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour will excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I now will read out the whole of these decisions. The first is on the Defence's application for an extension of time to apply for certification to appeal the Chamber's decision on the motion for acquittal. An application for certification is attached to the extension of time application. The Defence missed the seven-day deadline for certification. The Defence explains that it misunderstood the Rules, thinking that certification was not required in this case. The Defence relies on the decision in the Blagojevic case. However, in Blagojevic, what was at stake was a judgement of acquittal. It stands to reason that a judgement of acquittal, being final, does not require certification. In the present case, there was no judgement of acquittal. In the present case, the Chamber simply denied the Defence's interlocutory motion. There was no final judgement in any sense. In extending the Blagojevic ruling to the circumstances of the present case, the Defence misinterpreted that decision. The Defence should have proceeded on the assumption that the procedure for appealing interlocutory motions applied in this instance. The Blagojevic decision does reveal that there had been some confusion on this point in the past. The Defence could have raised the matter for clarification with the Chamber within the seven-day limit. The Defence has not shown good cause for an extension of time, as required by Rule 127. Therefore, we would deny this motion. The Chamber has also considered what its decision would have been had the Defence applied for a certificate in good time. The Defence submissions in favour of certification of the Chamber's 98 bis decisions are insufficiently detailed. The Chamber has consulted the Defence document that went before the Appeals Chamber in an effort to see what the arguments for certification might be. In that document, the Defence makes two complaints. One is the question of prejudice resulting from the Rule change. The Defence asserts that it would be, and I quote, "absurd and impractical, under the new Rule, to go through the contents of the indictment line by line." The Defence further asserts that, I quote: "The Trial Chamber would have correctly prevented such a course as being contrary to both the spirit and the letter of the new Rule." This conclusion about what the Trial Chamber would have done is entirely speculative. The fact is that the Defence did not make any request for line-by-line submissions. The lines in the indictment which the Defence did specifically attack, namely, the lines extending the charge of genocide to Bosnian Croats, were indeed considered by the Chamber, in the Defence's own specific terms. Clearly, the Chamber is in no position to certify a question about prejudice resulting from an imaginary ruling of the Chamber. The Defence simply does not know how the Chamber would have ruled in the face of a concrete request for detailed submissions. The Defence makes other assumptions too. It asserts that, I quote again: "It was incumbent upon the Trial Chamber itself to look at each and every part of the indictment, including the schedules, and see if there was evidence in support. This undoubtedly they did not do." Again, this is speculation. As a matter of fact, the Chamber has been doing, from the very beginning of this case, precisely what the Defence claims the Chamber has not done, so the Defence is simply wrong. In addition to this, the Defence clearly does not have to worry itself with unsupported allegations, the formal deletion of which would not have led to acquittal on any of the counts. The possibility that a limited number of such very specific, unsupported, factual allegations in the schedules has been carried past the 98 bis stage and into the Defence stage of the case, does not raise an issue of fairness or expeditiousness that meets the threshold of the certification test. The Defence's second complaint in the document it put before the Appeals Chamber is that the Trial Chamber did not cite sufficient evidence to justify keeping in place the allegation of genocide committed against Bosnian Croats. However, contrary to how the Defence sees it, the Trial Chamber merely presented a few illustrations, not the whole of the relevant evidence, in support of the allegation. The Trial Chamber is not obliged to specifically cite all the relevant evidence. Without doubt, it must take into account all the evidence when reaching its decision, but it need not to cite it specifically. Therefore, the Defence has not shown that the Chamber so exceeded its discretion in matters of factual appreciation as to have given rise to an issue appropriate for certification in accordance with the applicable test. Moreover, the presence or absence in the indictment of the allegation of genocide committed against Bosnian Croats is a variation that, in the Chamber's opinion, has little impact on the expeditiousness of these proceedings. The certification threshold is not met in this respect by them. Finally, the Defence claims that the Chamber erred in law in respect of the legal elements of genocide. This claim is completely without cited support. It cannot be the case that by merely questioning an aspect of the law, a party can create a ground for certification. The Defence's claim does not give rise to an issue that requires the intervention of the Appeals Chamber. This concludes the decision in relation to the first matter before us. The second decision concerns the Defence's application for a certificate to appeal the Chamber's denial of the Defence's motion for extension of time in which to comply with the requirements of Rule 65 ter (G). This extension of time entailed a delay in the commencement of the Defence case. In its original motion, the Defence had asked for three things: That its list of witnesses be received on the 12th of October; that the Defence not be obliged to file a list of exhibits by that date; and that the Defence case be rescheduled to commence on the 25th of October. The Chamber, in its decision, which the Defence now seeks leave to appeal, set the following schedule: A provisional list of witnesses, to be finalised progressively, was to be filed on the 3rd of October. The list of exhibits was not to be filed by that date but was to be disclosed progressively. And the Defence case was to commence on the 10th of October, for three days only, and then to restart on the 25th of October. Moreover, at the 73 ter conference last week, the Chamber further mitigated the burden of the Rules on the Defence by giving the Defence more time to produce acceptable summaries of the expected testimony of its witnesses. A necessary condition for the grant of a certificate is that the impugned decision gives rise to an issue which would significantly affect the fair and expeditious conduct of the proceedings or the outcome of the trial. The threshold is high. Considering the small differences between what the Defence requested and what it received through the decision in question, and considering also the point we have reached in the proceedings, namely, that the provisional list of witnesses has been filed and the Defence case has commenced with its first witness, in the Chamber's view, there does not exist an issue which justifies certification. Therefore, the Chamber will not allow the Defence's application. This concludes the Chamber's decision on the two Defence motions. We'll adjourn until the 25th of October, 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 25th day of October, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.
